 Two Years Requested, One Available: A Skincare Export Lesson for K-Beauty
 by 
 Daehyun Song 
 post_date_format( $post ) ); ?> 
 --> 
 November 7, 2026 
 in 
 Global Expansion 
 0 
 A skincare brand in Bali had what many emerging beauty companies work hard to secure: interest from overseas distributors. Yet a product specification threatened to hold back its expansion. The brand could reportedly offer one year of shelf life, while a prospective European distributor required two. Steven Ghoos , who leads commercialization at Singapore-based HydraX , shared the experience of this separate skincare business. The case raises an uncomfortable question for Korean beauty companies pursuing overseas expansion: What happens when international demand moves faster than a product’s ability to meet distribution requirements? 
 A Skincare Brand Found Overseas Interest, but Shelf Life Became the Obstacle
 The challenge emerged through an independent skincare business in Bali, Indonesia, which already sells directly to consumers and supplies resorts and salons . Despite its established domestic sales channels, the brand encountered a different requirement when exploring international distribution.
 Steven Ghoos , Co-Founder leading Commercialization and Go-to-Market at Singapore-based A*STAR spin-off HydraX , shared the case with KoreaTechDesk. His company develops plant-derived ingredient technology with potential skincare preservation applications, bringing him into contact with beauty businesses navigating formulation and shelf-life challenges. 
 “One brand has a ready to export partner that requires a 2 year minimum shelf life but can only do 1 year maximum currently,”
 Ghoos explained during his exclusive KoreaTechDesk interview on deep-tech commercialization .
 In subsequent correspondence, he elaborated that the Bali brand’s owner had attracted interest from a prospective European distributor, conditional on achieving a two-year product shelf life . A separate inquiry involving a Taiwanese distributor and a potential retail channel had reportedly encountered a similar requirement.
 These opportunities expose a commercial challenge that can emerge even after a beauty company has established its products and attracted potential overseas partners. Distributor interest does not automatically translate into market access when the finished product cannot yet meet the buyer’s specifications. 
 That is why the immediate question for the Bali brand extends beyond finding customers. Its ability to pursue these international distribution opportunities depends on demonstrating a longer product shelf life while maintaining the qualities that make its skincare products commercially appealing. 
 Illustration of K-beauty shelf display. | Stock Photo 
 Why Skincare Shelf Life Can Determine Distributor Acceptance
 The Bali brand’s experience reveals a practical challenge in international beauty distribution: a product’s remaining usable life can influence its commercial viability long before it reaches consumers. A distributor must account for the time products spend in transit, customs clearance, warehouses, and retail inventory before they are sold.
 According to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) , cosmetic shelf life refers to the period during which a product can be expected to remain safe and perform as intended . That period depends on the formulation, storage conditions, and exposure to environmental factors such as temperature and moisture. 
 For international buyers, the critical calculation often concerns how much verified shelf life remains when the shipment arrives. A product manufactured with a 12-month shelf life may have substantially less time available for retail distribution after transportation and storage. This can affect inventory acceptance, replenishment schedules, and the risk of holding products that approach expiration before they are sold.
 Consequently, a skincare product can satisfy its established safety and quality specifications yet still fall short of a particular distributor’s commercial requirements. Brands offering shorter shelf lives may need faster inventory turnover, smaller shipments, or alternative supply arrangements to make international distribution commercially workable.
 Illustration of officer checking K-beauty products on shelf. | Stock Photo 
 Some Buyers Set Requirements Beyond Cosmetics Regulations
 These commercial expectations can be written directly into a buyer’s supply agreement. Under the supplier terms published by UK-based Luxury Beauty Wholesale in August 2026 , products must generally have at least 24 months of remaining shelf life , or 75% of their total stated shelf life if shorter , when responsibility for the goods transfers to the buyer. Different arrangements may be agreed through the purchase order.
 The agreement also requires suppliers to provide batch identification, maintain appropriate storage and transportation conditions, and supply relevant product documentation . It allows the buyer to reject products that are deteriorated, approaching expiration, or otherwise fail to meet agreed specifications. Shelf lifetherefore becomes part of the contractual conditions governing inventory acceptance and supplier accountability . 
 For skincare exporters, such requirements can influence which distribution arrangements are commercially feasible . A product with a shorter validated shelf life may still be suitable for international sales, but its compatibility with a particular buyer depends on the remaining shelf life and conditions specified in the agreement. 
 The commercial lesson extends beyond the Bali brand’s experience. Attracting overseas interest is only one stage of market entry; securing distribution also requires a product that actually meets the prospective buyer’s operating requirements. Understanding those conditions early can help beauty brands make better decisions about production, shipment schedules, and international partnerships. 
 Illustration of discussion on contract and regulation. | Stock Photo 
 EU Cosmetics Regulations Do Not Impose a Universal Two-Year Shelf Life
 A distributor’s requirement for two years of shelf life should not be confused with a legal condition for entering the European cosmetics market.
 Under EU Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 , cosmetic products must meet applicable safety requirements, while Article 19 establishes specific labeling obligations concerning product durability.
 Products with a minimum durability of 30 months or less must display a minimum-durability date, indicating how long they remain safe and perform their intended function under appropriate storage conditions. Products lasting longer than 30 months generally do not require that date but must indicate the period after opening during which they can be used safely, where applicable.
 Crucially, EU cosmetics regulations do not establish a universal 24-month minimum shelf life for imported skincare products.
 In fact, individual distributors may actually impose stricter commercial conditions based on their inventory cycles, retail arrangements, and supply agreements. Those conditions can determine a product’s suitability for a particular sales channel even when it satisfies the applicable regulatory requirements.
 European market entry also involves notification through the European Commission’s Cosmetic Products Notification Portal (CPNP) . The system requires the designated responsible person to submit relevant product information before placing cosmetics on the EU market. However, this notification still does not replace the manufacturer’s safety obligations or constitute approval by prospective retail partners.
 It means that for Korean skincare exporters, regulatory compliance and commercial acceptance must therefore be addressed separately . Understanding a distributor’s exact shelf-life expectations, including how much usable life must remain upon delivery, can help brands assess potential distribution agreements before committing to international expansion.
 K-Beauty’s European Retail Expansion Raises the Importance of Product Readiness
 Korean skincare is gaining a stronger presence in established European retail networks, bringing product specifications and distribution requirements into sharper commercial focus. As brands expand beyond online sales and specialist beauty stores, their ability to satisfy local partners’ operating conditions becomes increasingly important.
 According to the Ministry of Food and Drug Safety’s October 2026 announcement , South Korean cosmetics exports reached approximately USD 11.1 billion during January–September 2026, up 31.1% year over year . The nine-month total approached the USD 11.4 billion recorded throughout 2025, reflecting the industry’s expanding international reach.
 Europe illustrates how this growth is reshaping distribution. An October 1 report by the Korea Trade-Investment Promotion Agency (KOTRA) found that Dutch imports of South Korean cosmetics under HS 3304 reached USD 165.67 million in 2025 , increasing 21.01% year over year and accounting for 6.71% of the Netherlands’ imports in that category.
 KOTRA documented Korean beauty products entering premium retailers, major drugstores, specialized online platforms, and natural-beauty channels. A local distributor interviewed by the agency identified EU product notification procedures, multilingual labeling, logistics costs, and retailer-specific assortment requirements among the challenges facing Korean cosmetics suppliers.
 The retail expansion extends into Belgium. In an October 14 market report , KOTRA highlighted drugstore chain Kruidvat’s June 2026 launch of eight private-label skincare products manufactured in South Korea. The development shows how Korean cosmetics manufacturing is becoming integrated into European retailers’ own product portfolios , alongside the international expansion of established Korean brands.
 These developments create new opportunities, but greater retail access also brings more demanding operational considerations .
 Shelf-life specifications are one example of how a product’s readiness can influence its compatibility with a prospective distribution partner. Smaller K-beauty exporters, in particular, need to understand such requirements early, since strong consumer interest alone cannot resolve limitations in the finished product or its supply arrangements.
 Longer Shelf Life Must Be Demonstrated in the Finished Skincare Product
 Meeting a distributor’s two-year shelf-life requirement involves more than introducing an ingredient with promising preservation properties. The finished skincare product must remain safe, stable, and capable of performing as intended throughout its claimed shelf life.
 According to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration ‘s guidance on cosmetic shelf life , cosmetics can deteriorate through microbial contamination, preservative breakdown, emulsion separation, and exposure to temperature, sunlight, or unsuitable storage conditions . These factors can affect a product’s safety, appearance, texture, and usability, even when its original formulation performs well under controlled conditions.
 The international standard ISO 11930:2019 provides a framework to evaluate antimicrobial protection in cosmetic formulations, while broader stability assessments help establish how finished products perform over time. The Irish Health Products Regulatory Authority also explains that declared minimum durability and period-after-opening information must be supported by evidence documented in the cosmetic product safety report.
 The commercial challenge becomes more demanding when extending shelf life risks changing the qualities consumers already value. 
 Ghoos explained that the Bali skincare brand would need a proposed preservation solution to demonstrate effectiveness while maintaining the finished product’s texture , an important consideration in consumer acceptance.
 A formulation that achieves longer durability but compromises the product’s established characteristics could introduce another obstacle to commercial growth. The real objective is to meet the distributor’s shelf-life requirement without sacrificing product quality or consumer experience. 
 As Korean skincare companies pursue increasingly established international retail channels, validated product stability becomes part of commercial readiness . A longer shelf-life claim gains business value when the finished product can substantiate that durability and continue delivering the experience customers expect.
 What Korean Skincare Exporters Should Establish Before Negotiating Distribution
 The Bali brand’s experience raises an important question that Korean skincare startups should address early in their export planning: Can the existing product meet the prospective distributor’s requirements without major changes to its formulation, production, or supply arrangements ? 
 A skincare line developed around domestic retail or direct-to-consumer sales may operate successfully under relatively short inventory cycles. Entering international wholesale, however, can introduce longer storage periods, larger shipment volumes, and contractual obligations that place different demands on product durability.
 Shelf-life expectations should therefore be established before distribution negotiations reach the purchasing stage. Korean exporters need to understand the minimum remaining shelf life required upon delivery, acceptable stability documentation, storage conditions, and how the distributor handles inventory approaching expiration. That is because these details can influence manufacturing schedules, shipment frequency, and the financial risks associated with unsold stock.
 If a product cannot meet the proposed conditions, extending its shelf life is not necessarily the only commercial response . Brands may investigate alternative packaging, adjust production and replenishment schedules, negotiate different inventory arrangements, or pursue distribution channels better suited to their existing product specifications. Each option carries different operational costs and must remain compatible with applicable safety and regulatory obligations. 
 The issue also affects how international expansion opportunities are evaluated. Distributor inquiries demonstrate potential market interest, but the feasibility of meeting the buyer’s conditions determines how readily that interest can develop into a commercial relationship. 
 Investors and startup-support organizations assessing K-beauty’s overseas growth should therefore look beyond prospective buyer counts and examine the product and supply capabilities needed to fulfill those opportunities.
 The Overseas Order May Be Decided Before the Sales Pitch
 Imagine a Korean skincare founder entering negotiations with a promising European distributor. The brand has consumer interest, an appealing product story, and a potential partner capable of placing it in stores, but the decisive question may concern a specification established long before the meeting. 
 How much of the product’s verified shelf life will remain when the distributor receives its inventory? 
 That question can influence the economics of expansion well before the first overseas sale. It can also reveal limitations in a product originally developed for a different sales model , even when the brand’s marketing and international positioning are commercially attractive.
 As Korean beauty companies pursue broader international distribution, their strongest opportunities may depend on recognizing these requirements before production decisions become difficult or expensive to change. 
 A distributor’s interest can open the conversation. The finished product’s documented capabilities help determine how far that conversation can go.
 Understanding exporter’s shelf-life gap. | AI infographic 
 Key Takeaway
 Skincare product shelf life can become a distribution requirement. Steven Ghoos of HydraX described a Bali skincare brand whose reported one-year shelf life falls short of a prospective overseas distributor’s two-year condition.
 Distributor interest does not guarantee an executable export opportunity. Product specifications, inventory conditions, and commercial acceptance requirements can affect market access even when a prospective buyer expresses interest.
 EU cosmetics regulations do not impose a universal two-year minimum shelf life. Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 governs cosmetic safety and durability labeling, while individual distributors can establish additional contractual requirements.
 Remaining shelf life at delivery can be commercially important. Published UK wholesale supply terms provide an example of a buyer requiring 24 months of remaining shelf life, with an alternative percentage requirement for shorter-lived products.
 K-beauty’s European expansion brings additional operational considerations. October 2026 KOTRA reporting identifies growing Korean beauty distribution through established European retail channels alongside compliance, logistics, and retailer-specific requirements.
 Cosmetic product stability must be supported by finished-product evidence. Preservation performance alone does not establish the full shelf life of a skincare formulation, and HydraX has not demonstrated a two-year outcome in the reported case.
 Korean skincare exporters should identify channel specifications early. Shelf-life requirements, acceptable documentation, shipment planning, and inventory obligations can influence product development and international distribution strategy.
